newsitem.title: ITALY: Olivetti head confirms contact on PC unit.
newsitem.headline: Olivetti head confirms contact on PC unit.

text.p: Olivetti is in talks to sell its ailing personal computer business, chief executive Roberto Colaninno said Wednesday.
"We are talking. There are contacts with the company that wants to buy," he told reporters in Rome after leaving a meeting of the Italian industrialists group Confindustria.
Colaninno would not name the company but at least two bidders are said to be in the running.

U.S. financier Edward Gottesman of the Centenary group is working on a bid with Zanussi chairman Gianmario Rossignolo while U.S. corporate debt trader Gary Klesch, head of London-based Klesch and Co., is also reported to be interested.
Newspapers and analysts estimated that a deal to sell Olivetti's troubled PC division could be worth around 200 billion lire ($130 million) in cash and debt reduction.

"Selling PCs is the first step, something the market was waiting for," said one Milan-based analyst. "But longer term there are still too many doubts on this company to say all the problems are over."
The Italian company, which also makes calculators, typewriters and other office products as well as furniture and computer accessories, has posted large losses the last several years.
Even stripping PCs from Olivetti's current results leaves Colaninno with a company unable to cover its financial charges, said Alberto Rolla, analyst at Milan broker Pasfin.
Marie-Christine Keith at James Capel in London said selling the PC business was a good first step.

"(Sale of the PC division) leaves Olivetti looking how they want it to look -- with systems and services at the moment supplying the bulk of the sales and OPI (mobile phones) the growing part of the business," Keith said.
But she expected further divestments would be necessary to reduce debt and make the group a leaner, meaner outfit.

A Milan analyst who declined to be named said profitability had deteriorated at the systems and services division and while the sector had reasonably good prospects in the next few years, "the problem is whether Olivetti can maintain competitiveness."
Fixed costs were too high, as were staffing levels. Clients signing new contracts needed to be sure Olivetti would still exist in a few years to fulfil those contracts, he said.
